# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

# Tool Responses

| Field  | Value |
| ------ | ----- |
| Issue  | n/a   |
| Status | Draft |

By default, a tool executor returns a plain string that feeds back into the AI conversation. The client never sees the result -- it only sees the tool invocation (name and input parameters). This is fine for most tools, but sometimes a tool knows exactly what to show the user and does not need the AI to rephrase it.

The `ToolResponse` interface gives tools two additional capabilities:

1. **Client messages** -- send one or more WebSocket messages directly to the client
2. **Suppress the AI response** -- keep the model's reply in conversation context but hide it from the client

These are opt-in. Tools that return a plain string continue to work exactly as before.

## The ToolResponse Interface

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolResponse -->
```typescript
interface ToolResponse {
  result: string;
  clientMessages?: OutgoingMessage[];
  suppressAssistantResponse?: boolean;
}
```

| Field | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `result` | The string the AI model sees -- identical to what a plain-string executor returns |
| `clientMessages` | Optional array of `OutgoingMessage` values sent directly to the client via WebSocket |
| `suppressAssistantResponse` | When `true`, the AI's next text response still accumulates in `session.entries` for context continuity, but is not sent to the client |

A `ToolExecutor` can return either a plain `string` or a `ToolResponse`:

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
```typescript
type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
```

`context` carries the session the call belongs to -- `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and the `authHeaders` forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade, so a tool can proxy the caller's credentials upstream.

The registry normalizes both forms internally via `normalizeToolResponse()`, so downstream code always sees a `ToolResponse`.

## When to Use This

**Client messages** make sense when the tool result is self-explanatory and the AI does not need to interpret it for the user. A unit conversion, a status update, a formatted data table -- these are cases where the tool knows the best presentation and the AI would just parrot the same information.

**Suppression** pairs naturally with client messages. If the tool already sent the answer to the client, the AI's follow-up ("The conversion result is 160.93 km") adds no value. Suppression hides that echo while keeping it in the conversation so the AI remembers the context for follow-up questions.

Use plain string returns (the default) when the AI needs to interpret or summarize the tool result for the user. Database lookups and search results are good examples -- the raw data benefits from the AI explaining it in context.

## Data Flow

```
Plain string:    executor returns "data"
                   -> normalizeToolResponse wraps to {result: "data"}
                   -> orchestrator feeds result to AI
                   -> AI responds, client sees the response

1	# Tool Responses
2	
3	| Field  | Value |
4	| ------ | ----- |
5	| Issue  | n/a   |
6	| Status | Draft |
7	
8	By default, a tool executor returns a plain string that feeds back into the AI conversation. The client never sees the result -- it only sees the tool invocation (name and input parameters). This is fine for most tools, but sometimes a tool knows exactly what to show the user and does not need the AI to rephrase it.
9	
10	The `ToolResponse` interface gives tools two additional capabilities:
11	
12	1. **Client messages** -- send one or more WebSocket messages directly to the client
13	2. **Suppress the AI response** -- keep the model's reply in conversation context but hide it from the client
14	
15	These are opt-in. Tools that return a plain string continue to work exactly as before.
16	
17	## The ToolResponse Interface
18	
19	<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolResponse -->
20	```typescript
21	interface ToolResponse {
22	  result: string;
23	  clientMessages?: OutgoingMessage[];
24	  suppressAssistantResponse?: boolean;
25	}
26	```
27	
28	| Field | Purpose |
29	|-------|---------|
30	| `result` | The string the AI model sees -- identical to what a plain-string executor returns |
31	| `clientMessages` | Optional array of `OutgoingMessage` values sent directly to the client via WebSocket |
32	| `suppressAssistantResponse` | When `true`, the AI's next text response still accumulates in `session.entries` for context continuity, but is not sent to the client |
33	
34	A `ToolExecutor` can return either a plain `string` or a `ToolResponse`:
35	
36	<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
37	```typescript
38	type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
39	```
40	
41	`context` carries the session the call belongs to -- `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and the `authHeaders` forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade, so a tool can proxy the caller's credentials upstream.
42	
43	The registry normalizes both forms internally via `normalizeToolResponse()`, so downstream code always sees a `ToolResponse`.
44	
45	## When to Use This
46	
47	**Client messages** make sense when the tool result is self-explanatory and the AI does not need to interpret it for the user. A unit conversion, a status update, a formatted data table -- these are cases where the tool knows the best presentation and the AI would just parrot the same information.
48	
49	**Suppression** pairs naturally with client messages. If the tool already sent the answer to the client, the AI's follow-up ("The conversion result is 160.93 km") adds no value. Suppression hides that echo while keeping it in the conversation so the AI remembers the context for follow-up questions.
50	
51	Use plain string returns (the default) when the AI needs to interpret or summarize the tool result for the user. Database lookups and search results are good examples -- the raw data benefits from the AI explaining it in context.
52	
53	## Data Flow
54	
55	```
56	Plain string:    executor returns "data"
57	                   -> normalizeToolResponse wraps to {result: "data"}
58	                   -> orchestrator feeds result to AI
59	                   -> AI responds, client sees the response
60	
61	With client messages:
62	                 executor returns {result, clientMessages, suppressAssistantResponse}
63	                   -> orchestrator extracts .result for AI (unchanged)
64	                   -> orchestrator yields tool_result chunk carrying clientMessages
65	                   -> if suppress, orchestrator yields suppress_output chunk
66	                   -> messageHandler sends clientMessages to client
67	                   -> messageHandler blanks pre-tool assistant entries (entry_upsert with empty content)
68	                   -> messageHandler skips WebSocket sends for suppressed entries
69	                   -> messageHandler sends entry_skip for each new suppressed entry
70	                   -> suppressed entries still accumulate in session.entries
71	                   -> client adjusts incoming indices using tracked skip list
72	```
73	
74	The key insight: suppressed entries are invisible to the client but visible to the AI. The conversation context stays intact, so the model can reference previous tool results even when the user did not see the AI's commentary on them.
75	
76	## Example: Unit Converter
77	
78	The `convert_units` tool demonstrates all three features: client messages, suppression, and index assignment. A conversion like "100 miles to kilometers" has a definitive answer -- the AI does not need to elaborate.
79	
80	<!-- doc-block: none -- a simplified tool, marked simplified in its own first line -->
81	```typescript
82	// src/orchestration/tools/unitConverterTool.ts (simplified)
83	
84	export const executeUnitConverter: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {
85	  const value = input.value as number;
86	  const fromUnit = (input.from_unit as string) || '';
87	  const toUnit = (input.to_unit as string) || '';
88	
89	  const result = convert(value, fromUnit, toUnit);
90	
91	  if (!result) {
92	    // Error case: return plain string so AI can explain the problem
93	    return JSON.stringify({error: `Cannot convert from "${fromUnit}" to "${toUnit}".`});
94	  }
95	
96	  return {
97	    result: JSON.stringify({value, fromUnit, toUnit, converted: result.converted, formatted: result.formatted}),
98	    clientMessages: [
99	      {
100	        type: 'entry_upsert',
101	        index: 0,
102	        entry: {role: 'assistant', content: result.formatted, timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), isStreaming: false},
103	      },
104	    ],
105	    suppressAssistantResponse: true,
106	  };
107	};
108	```
109	
110	Notice three things:
111	
112	1. On success, the executor returns a `clientMessages` array with an `entry_upsert` containing the formatted result. The client receives this as an assistant entry. The `index` is set to `0` -- the orchestrator replaces it with the correct session index (see "Index assignment" below).
113	
114	2. `suppressAssistantResponse: true` hides the AI's follow-up. The AI still receives the result string (so it has context for follow-ups), but the client does not see the AI echoing "100 miles equals 160.93 km."
115	
116	3. On error, the executor returns a plain string. This lets the AI explain what went wrong in its own words -- "I could not convert miles to knots because they measure different things."
117	
118	## Adding Client Messages
119	
120	If the tool wants to send a custom message to the client, use `clientMessages`. Any valid `OutgoingMessage` type works -- `entry_upsert`, `entry_delta`, `entry_commit`, or `error`.
121	
122	<!-- doc-block: none -- a worked executor showing one return shape, not code this package exports -->
123	```typescript
124	export const executeMyTool: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {
125	  const data = await fetchSomething(input);
126	
127	  return {
128	    result: JSON.stringify(data),
129	    clientMessages: [
130	      {type: 'entry_upsert', index: 0, entry: {
131	        role: 'assistant' as const,
132	        content: formatData(data),
133	        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
134	        isStreaming: false,
135	      }},
136	    ],
137	  };
138	};
139	```
140	
141	Client messages are forwarded to the WebSocket after index assignment. The client processes them through its existing message dispatch pipeline -- no client-side changes needed.
142	
143	### Index assignment for entry_upsert
144	
145	Tools do not have access to the session, so they cannot know the correct entry index. The orchestrator handles this automatically: any `entry_upsert` message in `clientMessages` gets its `index` replaced with the real value by appending the entry to the session. The tool can set `index` to any value -- it will be overwritten.
146	
147	This means the entry also becomes part of the session's `entries` array, maintaining context continuity for the AI model.
148	
149	## How It Works Under the Hood
150	
151	### Orchestrator
152	
153	After executing tool calls, `chatOrchestrator.ts` checks each `ToolResponse` for client messages and suppression flags:
154	
155	<!-- doc-block: none -- the orchestrator fragment that normalises responses, quoted out of its function -->
156	```typescript
157	const responses = await Promise.all(
158	  pendingToolCalls.map(async (tc) => {
159	    const response = await toolRegistry.execute(tc.name, tc.input);
160	    return {tc, response};
161	  })
162	);
163	
164	// Collect client messages from all tools
165	const clientMessages = responses.flatMap(({response}) => response.clientMessages ?? []);
166	
167	// Yield them as a chunk for the message handler
168	if (clientMessages.length > 0) {
169	  yield {type: 'tool_result', clientMessages};
170	}
171	
172	// Signal suppression if any tool requested it
173	if (responses.some(({response}) => response.suppressAssistantResponse)) {
174	  yield {type: 'suppress_output'};
175	}
176	```
177	
178	### Message Handler
179	
180	Two new chunk types flow through `processChunk`:
181	
182	- `tool_result` -- each client message in the array is serialized and sent directly to the WebSocket
183	- `suppress_output` -- sets `state.suppressOutput = true` on the stream state
184	
185	When suppression is active, `streamSegment` and `commitAndClear` still call `appendEntry`, `appendDelta`, and `commitEntry` (so the session accumulates entries for context), but skip `sendUpsert`, `sendDelta`, and `sendCommit` (so the client sees nothing).
186	
187	When a new entry is created under suppression, the server sends an `entry_skip` message with the server-side index. This tells the client "an entry exists here on the server, but you will never receive it." The client tracks these skipped indices and adjusts all subsequent incoming indices via the `adjustIndex` pure function. Without this, server indices would diverge from the client's entry array, causing deltas and commits to target the wrong positions.
188	
189	If the AI streamed text *before* the tool call (which happens when the model explains what it is about to do), that text was already sent to the client as an assistant entry. When suppression activates, the server retroactively blanks these entries by sending `entry_upsert` with empty content. The client already skips rendering empty assistant entries, so the pre-tool text disappears cleanly.
190	
191	**Suppression is sticky for the entire stream.** Once a tool sets `suppressAssistantResponse: true` in any round, all subsequent AI responses in that stream are suppressed -- even if later tool rounds do not set the flag. This is intentional: suppression is a per-message property, not per-round. If the first tool already sent the definitive answer to the client, the AI's commentary in all following rounds is equally redundant. A new user message starts a fresh stream with `suppressOutput: false`.
192	
193	### stream_end and the spinner
194	
195	The server sends a `stream_end` message after every completed stream (see [websocket-protocol.md](../hal-engine-websocket-protocol/spec.md)). This is the client's signal to clear loading indicators.
196	
197	Without `stream_end`, suppression would cause the tool spinner to hang forever. When the assistant response is suppressed, no `entry_upsert` arrives after the tool entry, so the tool stays as the last entry in the array. The client tracks an `isProcessing` state: `true` when the user sends a message, `false` when `stream_end` arrives. The spinner only shows when the tool is both last in the list *and* the stream is still processing.
198	
199	### MessageChunk union
200	
201	The `MessageChunk` type gained two variants:
202	
203	<!-- doc-block: src/types/ai.ts#MessageChunk -->
204	```typescript
205	type MessageChunk =
206	  | {type: 'text'; text: string}
207	```
208	
209	These two variants are internal plumbing -- they never leave the server. The client only sees standard `OutgoingMessage` types over the WebSocket.
210	
211	## File Reference
212	
213	| File | What changed |
214	|------|-------------|
215	| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolResponse` interface, widened `ToolExecutor`, `normalizeToolResponse()` |
216	| `src/types/ai.ts` | `tool_result` and `suppress_output` variants on `MessageChunk` |
217	| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | `executeToolCalls` returns `ToolExecutionResult`, yields new chunks |
218	| `src/transport/ws/messageHandler.ts` | `suppressOutput` on stream state, `processToolResultChunk`, guarded sends, `entry_skip`, blanking |
219

8	This document walks through how the hal-engine system works, from the moment a user types a message to the moment they see a streaming response.
9	
10	## The Big Picture
11	
12	The system has three layers: a frontend client, a Node.js backend (hal-engine), and a pluggable AI provider. They communicate over WebSocket for real-time streaming.
13	
14	Only the middle layer is this repository. The `Client` group below, the `applyUpsert`/`applyDelta`/`applyCommit` functions in Entry Streaming Protocol, the reconnection and unmount behaviour under Connection Lifecycle, and the spinner logic in Tool Execution Loop all describe a browser client. They are here because the protocol only makes sense as a pair, not because any of it ships from here.
15

# Architecture

| Field  | Value       |
| ------ | ----------- |
| Issue  | n/a         |
| Status | In Progress |

This document walks through how the hal-engine system works, from the moment a user types a message to the moment they see a streaming response.

## The Big Picture

The system has three layers: a frontend client, a Node.js backend (hal-engine), and a pluggable AI provider. They communicate over WebSocket for real-time streaming.

Only the middle layer is this repository. The `Client` group below, the `applyUpsert`/`applyDelta`/`applyCommit` functions in Entry Streaming Protocol, the reconnection and unmount behaviour under Connection Lifecycle, and the spinner logic in Tool Execution Loop all describe a browser client. They are here because the protocol only makes sense as a pair, not because any of it ships from here.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Client
        CC[ChatContainer]
        WS[WebSocket Client]
        MD[MessageDisplay]
    end

    subgraph "hal-engine"
        CH[connectionHandler]
        MH[messageHandler]
        CO[chatOrchestrator]
        PB[promptBuilder]
        TR[toolRegistry]
    end

    subgraph "AI Provider"
        AI[Bedrock / Vertex / OpenAI / Anthropic / Mock]
    end

    CC --> WS
    WS -->|WebSocket| CH
    CH --> MH
    MH --> CO
    CO --> AI
    CO --> PB
    CO --> TR
    TR -->|promptInstructions| PB
    TR -->|examplePrompts| CH
    WS --> MD
```
